Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Review the basic science and terminology related to musculoskeletal ultrasonography.
Implement diagnostic ultrasonography as an imaging modality for musculoskeletal conditions.
Recognize normal and pathologic ultrasonographic images.
Compare various types of ultrasonographic-guided procedures and the rationale for their use.

Musculoskeletal ultrasonography is used for diagnosis of neuromusculoskeletal
pathology and to guide diagnostic and therapeutic interventions. According to an
updated consensus by the European Society for Skeletal Radiology in 2018,
ultrasonography can be used to diagnose 70 conditions for which another imaging
modality rarely provides additional information1 (Resource 1). Recent evidence also
suggests that ultrasonographic-guided injections are more accurate and efficacious than
landmark-guided injections2 (Resource 2). In addition, ultrasonography can be used to
guide more advanced injections and procedures that may be able to replace classical
surgical techniques. Orthopaedic surgeons should understand the basic science of
ultrasonography, outline the normal and abnormal appearance of musculoskeletal
structures, and provide information on the indications and fundamental techniques for
ultrasonographic-guided interventions.
Basics of Ultrasonography
Equipment
A standard ultrasonography unit consists of an image display monitor, a computer processing
unit, and an ultrasonographic transducer.
Image Generation
Sound waves emitted from the transducer are reflected off tissue interfaces that are being
imaged.
A crystal contained within the transducer converts waves to an electrical signal via the
piezoelectric effect, and this signal is used to create an image displayed on the monitor.
Ultrasonographic gel is used as a medium to transmit sound waves to and from the transducer
and the soft tissues.

Image Generation
A standard ultrasonography unit consists of three basic components: a computer
processing unit, an ultrasonographic transducer, and an image display monitor. Images

9/3/26, 7:51 AM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002094
2/57

are produced when sound waves are emitted, reflected off tissues, and converted to an
electrical signal that is then displayed on a monitor. The piezoelectric effect allows for
conversion of electrical energy into mechanical energy and vice versa.3 Traditional
ultrasonography units contain a small piezoelectric crystal in the head of the transducer
that generates the sound waves for imaging purposes. The use of ultrasonographic gel is
necessary as a medium to allow for efficient transmission of sound waves to and from
body tissues of interest (Resource 3).
Echogenicity
Structures are described in terms of brightness or echogenicity relative to their adjacent
surrounding tissues.
Hyperechoic structures appear bright relative to their surrounding tissues.
Hypoechoic structures appear dark relative to surrounding tissues
Isoechoic structures appear equal in brightness to surrounding tissues.
Anechoic structures appear completely black, indicating complete absence of echo.

Echogenicity
Ultrasonographic images are described in terms of brightness or echogenicity relative to
adjacent surrounding tissues. Hyperechoic and hypoechoic structures appear relatively
bright or relatively dark, respectively, to surrounding structures. Isoechoic structures
appear equal in brightness to surrounding tissues, and anechoic structures are
completely black, indicating absence of echo signal.
Image Quality and Optimization
High-frequency waves with short wavelength provide high-resolution images of relatively
superficial structures.
Low-frequency waves have a longer wavelength and can penetrate tissues to a greater depth.
Transducer selection
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:51 AM
AAOS | Diagnostic Ultrasonography and Ultrasonographic-Guided Procedures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002094
3/57

Curvilinear transducers emit relatively lower-frequency waves and are suitable for imaging
deeper body structures, such as the hip joint.
Linear transducers emit waves suitable for intermediate depth structures with more linear
architecture, such as ligaments or tendons
Small footprint transducers emit high-frequency waves and are best for imaging superficial
structures. The small footprint transducer is useful for imaging small irregular surfaces of the
distal extremities, such as the foot or hand.
Image depth, focal zone, and gain
Depth adjustment allows the user to center the structure of interest on the display. Maximal
depth varies between transducers.
Focal zone adjustment allows the user to optimize resolution over the region of interest.
Gain adjustment allows the user to increase or decrease overall brightness of the image.

Image Quality and Optimization
Image quality and resolution is heavily influenced by the wavelength and frequency
sound waves.3 High-frequency, short wavelength sound waves provide high-resolution
images; however, they have a limited depth of tissue penetration. Low-frequency, long
wavelength sound waves have a greater depth of penetration but at the expense of
image resolution. Therefore, selection of an ultrasonographic transducer that can
produce sound waves with an appropriate frequency and wavelength for a given
structure of interest is important for optimizing the image that is ultimately produced.
Curvilinear transducers are relatively low-frequency transducers suitable for imaging
deep body structures, such as the hip joint. Linear transducers are suitable for
intermediate-depth structures with more linear architecture, such as ligaments or
tendons. Small footprint transducers emit high-frequency waves and are best for
imaging small superficial structures, such as the hand or foot. Some ultrasonography
units also may have functions that allow the user to adjust certain properties of the
image, such as image depth, focal zone, and gain. These functions can be used to further
optimize the image appearance based on the structure of interest.
Appearance of Normal Structures

Tendons appear hyperechoic with fibrillar echotexture.
Muscle appears as hypoechoic bundles surrounded by thin hyperechoic septa.
Bone appears strongly hyperechoic.
Hyaline cartilage is hypoechoic and uniform in appearance.
Ligaments are hyperechoic and striated in appearance.
Nerves appear as hypoechoic fascicles surrounded by hyperechoic epineurium.

Appearance of Normal Structures
Normal healthy tissues have a characteristic appearance that is important to recognize
to determine if pathology is present.4 Tendons appear hyperechoic with fibrillar
echotexture (Figure 1). Muscle appears as hypoechoic bundles surrounded by thin
hyperechoic septa (Figures 2 and 3). Bones appear as strongly hyperechoic linear
structures (Figure 4). Cartilage is hypoechoic and uniform in appearance (Figure 5).
Ligaments are hyperechoic and striated in appearance and typically appear slightly more
compact than tendons (Figure 6). Nerves appear as hypoechoic fascicles surrounded by
hyperechoic epineurium (Figure 7).

Common Ultrasonographic Artifacts
Structures with anisotropy exhibit variable appearance if the ultrasonographic beam is
directed at different angles. Tendons appear characteristically hyperechoic with fibrillar
echotexture if the ultrasonographic beam is directed at a 90° angle to the tendon; however,
the tendon may appear more hypoechoic if the transducer is toggled a few degrees in any
direction.
Reverberation appears as a series of linear echoes deep to smooth, flat, and highly echogenic
structures.
Shadowing appears as a relatively hypoechoic region deep to a structure that refracts or
attenuates sound beams away from the transducer.
Increased through transmission appears as a relatively hyperechoic region deep to a structure
that weakly attenuates sound waves.

Common Ultrasonographic Artifacts
Sonographic artifacts are commonly encountered and are important to recognize so
they are not confused with pathology. Structures that exhibit anisotropy exhibit variable
appearance if the ultrasonographic beam is directed at different angles.5 Tendons
appear characteristically hyperechoic with fibrillar echotexture if the ultrasonographic
beam is directed at a 90° angle to the tendon; however, the tendon may appear more
hypoechoic if the transducer is toggled a few degrees in any direction (Figure 8).
Reverberation artifact appears as a series of linear echoes deep to smooth, flat, and
highly echogenic structures.6 This may occur deep to structures, such as bone, or
metallic objects, such as surgical hardware (Figure 9). Shadowing artifact appears as a
relatively hypoechoic region deep to a structure that refracts or attenuates sound beams
away from the transducer6 (Figure 10). Increased through transmission refers to a
relatively hyperechoic region deep to a structure that weakly attenuates sound waves,
such as a fluid collection or blood vessel6 (Figure 11).

Doppler Imaging
Doppler imaging modes are used to detect motion toward or away from a fixed point. Power
Doppler displays motions as color on the screen and is useful for identifying large vessels,
inflammation, or neovessel formation.

Doppler Imaging
Doppler imaging modes are another useful function of most ultrasonography units that
detects motions toward or away from a fixed point. Power Doppler displays motions as
color on the screen and is useful for displaying blood vessels, inflammation, or
neovascularization4 (Figure 12).

Pathology
Tendon
Acute Tear/Rupture
Hypoechoic or anechoic regions where tendon tissue should exist
Hematoma formation appears anechoic initially, becomes isoechoic as coagulation progresses
Marked hyperemia on color/power Doppler if acute
Chronic Tendon Tears
Hypoechoic or anechoic regions where tendon tissue should exist
Less likely hematoma formation compared with acute tear
Partial tears may appear similar to anechoic or hypoechoic regions within otherwise normal or
tendinopathic tendon.
Dynamic movement of the body part may help to determine the extent of the tear
Tendinosis
Hypoechoic, thickened with loss of normal fibrillar architecture
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002094
15/57

May demonstrate hyperemia on color Doppler
Dissimilar from partial tears, tendinosis usually displaces surrounding tissue because of
swelling (ie, subacromial bursa is displaced away from humeral head).
Tenosynovitis
Thickened tendon sheath
Painful with ultrasonographic palpation
Hyperemia noted with color Doppler
Tendon may be normal appearing

Tendon
Tendon pathology can be subdivided into acute and chronic tendon damage. Acute
tendon rupture may be well visualized with ultrasonography, especially if the tendon is
relatively superficial. The classic ultrasonographic appearance of an acute tendon
rupture is an anechoic region in the place of normal tendon tissue.4 The two ends of the
tendon often can be visualized; however, edge artifact may be a sign that complete tear
is present if the tendon ends cannot be observed.7 Hyperechoic bony fragments may be
observed in patients with an avulsion (Figure 13). Hematoma formation is common after
an acute tendon rupture and acutely appears as a hypoechoic or anechoic fluid
collection that becomes more hyperechoic with time. A dynamic examination may be
helpful in distinguishing between a partial- and full-thickness tendon rupture.

Figure 13 Long axis ultrasonographic image of a quadriceps tendon (left is distal) shows
a full-thickness tear with a piece of the patella avulsed off (arrow). The anechoic region
(stars) shows the location at which the tendon should be, and the hyperechoic fragment
of the patella can be observed on the right side of the screen. (Courtesy of Zachary
Bailowitz, MD, Oakland, CA.)
Chronic tendon changes also are well visualized. Tendinosis on ultrasonography shows
thickening of the tendon with a disorganized and hypoechoic appearance of the
otherwise fibrillar architecture of tendon tissue (Figure 14). Color or power Doppler
examination may show hyperemia of the tendon, indicating the presence of neovessels
(Figure 15); however, their absence does not rule out the diagnosis of tendinosis. Partial-
thickness tears are observed as anechoic clefts within surrounding tendon tissue. For
example, within the rotator cuff, partial-thickness tears can be diagnosed via
ultrasonography and via MRI,1 and can be distinguished as bursal-sided, articular-sided,
or intrasubstance (Figure 16). If the static ultrasonographic image is unclear, a dynamic
examination may help to distinguish full-thickness tear from a partial-thickness tear.

Figure 16 Short axis ultrasonographic image of a supraspinatus tendon (left is anterior)
shows an anechoic cleft measuring 1.42 cm, which is consistent with an articular-sided

Tenosynovitis may be observed as synovial thickening and/or anechoic or mixed
echogenicity fluid within the sheath (Figure 17). Normative values of tendon sheath
thickness generally are not well established; therefore, comparison with the
contralateral side often is used. The tendon itself may be tendinopathic; however, a
normal tendon also may be observed in patients with tenosynovitis.4 Color or power
Doppler examination shows hyperemia of the tendon sheath. This may help distinguish
true tenosynovitis from a dependent effusion, such as in patients with proximal biceps
tendon sheath fluid (Figure 18).

Ligament
Sprain/Partial Tear
Partial discontinuity of the visualized ligament, consisting of hypoechoic regions if acute and
thickening of the ligament if chronic
Complete Tear
Complete discontinuity of the ligament
Dynamic examination reveals gapping of the joint.

22/57

Compare with contralateral limb if applicable

Ligament
Ligament injuries are graded I through III depending on their severity. Grade I ligament
sprains may appear as hypoechoic thickening of the ligament with alteration of the linear
arrangement of the fibers and surrounding hyperemia on Doppler examination. Grade II
ligament tears show an anechoic region, indicating fiber disruption, but some normal
ligament remains (Figure 19). Grade III ligament tears are observed as complete fiber
disruption and usually are accompanied by gapping of the structure in question on
dynamic examination. The dynamic evaluation becomes particularly useful in these
patients to determine the amount of instability. For example, in patients with an elbow
ulnar collateral ligament injury, stress ultrasonography was found to be 96% sensitive
and 81% specific for the diagnosis of full-thickness ligament tears.8 Ulnar collateral
ligament thickening and calcification may be observed on ultrasonographic images of
young professional throwing athletes and may not be a specific indication of pathology
but rather evidence of ligament adaptation to increased stress.9
Figure 19 Long axis ultrasonographic image of the proximal portion of a medial
collateral ligament (left is proximal) shows a thickened and heterogenous ligament

Muscle
Acute Injuries
Grade I: often not appreciated on ultrasonography; however, may appear slightly hyperechoic
Grade II: partial disruption of fibers with hypoechoic or anechoic hemorrhage
Grade III: complete disruption of fibers with hypoechoic or anechoic hemorrhage; may show
muscle retraction
Chronic Injuries
As muscle injuries progress, hyperechoic scarring fills in.
Hemorrhage becomes more hyperechoic, starting at the periphery.
Myositis ossificans: can visualize early mineralization in healing tear, often before it can be
observed on radiographs
Atrophy: increased echogenicity, loss of striations, decreased muscle size

Muscle
Muscle injuries are graded I through III, with grade I representing minimal disruption of
muscle fibers, grade II representing macroscopic disruption of muscle fibers with some
remaining intact, and grade III representing complete muscle rupture.4 Grade I injuries
may appear normal on ultrasonography or show ill-defined hyperechoic regions. Grade II
injuries are marked by focal hypoechoic regions and discontinuity of the normal striated
echotexture. Grade III injuries reveal complete fiber disruption. Grade II and grade III
injuries typically are associated with anechoic hematoma formation (Figure 20). Having
the patient perform a muscle contraction may further define the degree of injury. As the
hematoma resolves over time, it will become more echogenic, starting at the periphery.
Chronic muscle injuries typically do not have associated hematoma; however,
hyperechoic scarring and fiber disruption usually is evident, especially in patients with
higher-grade injuries (Figure 21). Ultrasonography also may be helpful in the diagnosis

Joint
Osteoarthritis
Articular cartilage loss
Osteophytes are bony enlargements at the periarticular bone.
Can visualize joint effusions with or without synovitis
Rheumatoid Arthritis
Synovial hypertrophy: usually hypoechoic tissue within joint
Color Doppler examination may show active synovitis.
Bony erosions may be observed as cortical irregularities of the periarticular bone.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002094

Gout
Double-contour sign is uric acid crystals forming on the surface of articular cartilage.
Tophi appear as hyperechoic regions with a hypoechoic halo.
May also observe cortical erosions, joint effusions

Joint
Evaluations of joint pathology may be limited with ultrasonography given the inability to
penetrate bone and, therefore, provide views of intra-articular pathology; however,
ultrasonography still has utility in the evaluation of joint pathology. Some osteoarthritis
features observed on radiographs may be observed via ultrasonography, including joint-
space narrowing, periarticular osteophytes, and cortical irregularities (Figure 22).11
Ultrasonography also allows for visualization of thinning of articular cartilage in some
locations. Joint effusions and synovitis also may be observed with ultrasonography;
however, these findings are nonspecific.
Figure 22 Long axis ultrasonographic image of a medial knee joint line showsSEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:51 AM
AAOS | Diagnostic Ultrasonography and Ultrasonographic-Guided Procedures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002094
27/57

periarticular osteophytes, a slightly protruded meniscus, and cortical irregularities of the
proximal tibia, all of which are consistent with osteoarthritis. (Courtesy of Zachary
Bailowitz, MD, Oakland, CA.)
Dissimilar from osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis is an inflammatory and erosive
process. The typical features of rheumatoid arthritis on ultrasonographic images are
synovial hypertrophy and bony erosions. Synovial hypertrophy typically shows
hypoechoic tissue within a joint recess that is not compressible, and color/power
Doppler evaluation may show hyperemia (Figure 23). These features help distinguish
synovial hypertrophy from a simple effusion. The findings on ultrasonography can be
used not only to diagnose rheumatoid arthritis but also to monitor disease progression
and treatment efficacy. Similarly, gout may show signs of erosion and joint effusion, with
the additional findings of tophi. In addition, uric acid crystals may deposit on the surface
of articular cartilage, revealing the classic double-contour sign.4 This is in contrast to
pseudogout, in which the calcium pyrophosphate crystals are observed within the
cartilage.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 7:51 AM
AAOS | Diagnostic Ultrasonography and Ultrasonographic-Guided Procedures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002094

Figure 23 Long axis ultrasonographic image of a subacromial bursa shows substantial
hyperemic changes of the bursa and the supraspinatus tendon on power Doppler and a
large effusion within the bursa. (Courtesy of Eric Chen, MD, Seattle, WA.)
Evaluation of intra-articular fibrocartilage structures, such as the labrum or the
meniscus, is limited with ultrasonography; however, some evidence suggests that it may
be helpful in certain circumstances. Ultrasonography has been reliable in measuring
meniscal extrusions compared with MRI,12 which may be helpful in considering mass
effect from extruded material or parameniscal cysts. Techniques also have been
described to evaluate labral injuries;13,14 however, in general, they are thought to be less
accurate than MRI or magnetic resonance arthrography. In the opinion of the authors of
this lesson, ultrasonography is a useful tool for the initial evaluation of these types of
injuries (Figure 24); however, MRI should be the preferred imaging modality for the
diagnosis of fibrocartilage pathology.

Peripheral nerve pathology is one of the more useful applications of ultrasonography
because few other imaging modalities can provide as much detail as ultrasonography.
Entrapment neuropathies specifically have characteristic features that are well-defined
on ultrasonography. Typical findings include focal nerve enlargement just proximal to
the site of entrapment (Figure 25), fascicular architecture of the nerve, and decreased
echogenicity4,15 (Figure 26). Most measurements are taken in short axis to the nerve,
and cross-sectional area, measured inside the epineurium, is the most widely used
assessment of nerve size.14 Normative values exist for some common entrapment
neuropathies; however, the nerve often is compared with that of the contralateral limb
for assessment of pathology.

Overview
Compared with palpation-guided procedures, ultrasonographic-guided procedures offer
several advantages, including real-time evaluation and visualization of the needle and
area of concern. Visualization allows for precise targeting of the structure of interest,
contributing to improved accuracy of injectate.23-25 This improved accuracy has been
shown to result in improved efficacy of injections23,26 and is associated with a lower
complication rate. Compared with other image-guided techniques, ultrasonography
affords visualization of soft-tissue structures, which is not possible via fluoroscopic-
guided injections; requires less procedural time than CT-guided procedures; and can be
performed in the office at the point of care. Ultrasonography also is easily portable, is
not associated with ionizing radiation, and is associated with relatively low costs
compared with other image-guided techniques. Ultrasonographic-guided interventions
are associated with several limitations, including a steep learning curve resulting in
substantial operator dependency. Other limitations include the inability of sound waves
to penetrate bone, which makes intra-articular visualization difficult and affords
relatively poor visualization of very deep structures.

Needle Guidance
Several techniques are available for performing ultrasonographic-guided procedures.
Procedures can be indirect, in which a structure is visualized, depth is determined, and
the skin is marked directly over the area. Then, the probe is removed, and a needle is
guided perpendicularly into the target without visualization. This works well for
superficial structures but is not the preferred technique for most patients. Direct
procedures allow for simultaneous visualization of the needle and the target structure
and have two common approaches: in-plane and out-of-plane approaches. The in-plane
approach is the preferred technique for most patients because it allows for visualization
of the target structure and the entire needle throughout the entire procedure. In this
technique, the needle is inserted into the skin in parallel to the transducer and advanced
to the target. If using the out-of-plane approach, the needle is inserted perpendicular to
the transducer and advanced until the tip is visualized on ultrasonography. The needle is
then retracted and redirected deeper via a step-down technique until the tip is visualized
at the target structure. This technique allows for visualization of only a small segment of
the needle, only as it passes through the sound beam, resulting in the remainder of the
needle not being visualized. The out-of-plane technique generally is preferred only for
very superficial structures, such as the small joints in the hand and foot.

Site Preparation
Patient positioning is an important consideration to optimize the procedure. Most
procedures should be performed with the patient lying down and placed in the supine,
prone, or lateral recumbent position. This may help prevent vasovagal reactions, which
are common with injections. The target of interest should be visualized via
ultrasonography, and the approach, including site of entry and the angle of the
approach, should be planned before preparing the site and the administration of
medications. Marking the skin at the planned needle entry point will help to quickly
return to the target site.
Transducer selection is important before proceeding with injections. Linear transducers
with frequency higher than 10 MHz provide higher resolution for superficial structures

linear transducers, and deeper structures of the shoulder and hip should be approached

The size and depth of the target will determine the appropriate size needle. Lower-gauge
needles are more easily visualized on ultrasonography but cause more local tissue

After identifying the target and concerning adjacent structures and determining the
depth and optimal approach, the site must be prepared. Marking the skin at the needle
entry point will help to quickly return to the target site. The skin should then be cleansed
with the use of a topical cleanser (chlorhexidine, povidone-iodine, etc.). Gel should be
placed directly on the transducer, and sterile gloves should be donned. A sterile field
should be established with drapes or towels around the injection site, and a sterile
probe cover should be placed over the gel-covered transducer. Sterile gel may then be
placed directly on the skin or over the transducer.

Avoid moving the needle and transducer simultaneously to improve visualization.

Needle Visualization
For in-plane procedures, as the needle enters the skin, provide local anesthesia
subcutaneously. To ensure optimal visualization during in-plane procedures, the needle
should enter the skin directly parallel with the transducer. Advance the needle until it is
visualized on the screen. If the needle cannot be visualized after entering the skin,
translate the transducer along the skin to visualize the needle tip. After the tip is
identified, relocate the target structure and make any correction in needle path
necessary until the needle and the target are visualized on the same image. Ideally, the
entire needle will be visible throughout the procedure; however, care must be taken to
visualize the tip of the needle at a minimum. Looking from the screen to your hands to
ensure parallel trajectory of the needle with the transducer is important and may help
with needle visualization during in-plane procedures. If the needle cannot be visualized,
advancement of the needle should be stopped and the transducer should be translated
until the needle is visualized. After the needle is relocated, advancement to the target
may resume.
Several techniques are available to improve visualization. Larger-bore needles are easier
to visualize. Wiggling the needle as the transducer is being translated over it may aid in
visualization. Entering the skin farther from the probe and advancing in a shallower path
prevents refraction artifact and improves conspicuity. Heel-toeing the transducer away
from you also may bring the transducer and needle in parallel and improve visualization.
If the needle and transducer are not in parallel alignment, rotating the transducer
clockwise and counterclockwise may bring the entire needle into view. If the needle is
identified and the target structure can no longer be visualized, retracting the needle
slightly and relocating the target and the needle in same field of view may optimize the
approach.
For out-of-plane procedures, visualize the target structure in the center of the image.
With the needle entry point perpendicular to the probe, enter the skin approximately 1
cm from the probe at the midline of the transducer and advance until a portion of the
needle is visualized with the target in view. Retract the needle and redirect it in a steeper
approach until the needle is then visualized again on the image. Continue this process

Ultrasonographic-Guided Procedures
Musculoskeletal and sports ultrasonographic procedures are defined by three
generations (Resource 4).27 First-generation procedures include using ultrasonographic
guidance to improve the accuracy of common and established procedures, such as joint
injections, tendon sheath injections, and perineural injections. These commonly include
corticosteroid injections, viscosupplementation injections, and regenerative medicine
injections. Second-generation procedures have emerged more recently and are
considered advanced needle-based procedures. These procedures include
ultrasonographic-guided tenotomy/fasciotomy, nerve hydrodissection, A1 pulley release,
and barbotage of calcific tendinitis. Tenotomies are commonly combined with
regenerative medicine (platelet-rich plasma, bone marrow aspirate concentrate, etc.).
Third-generation procedures use preexisting or proprietary surgical instruments to
perform specific procedures. These procedures duplicate accepted surgical procedures
percutaneously in an outpatient setting and may help to reduce morbidity, recovery
time, and costs. These procedures include the use of hook knives and cutting thread for

Summary/Outcomes
Ultrasonography is a useful imaging modality for diagnosis and to guide management of
musculoskeletal pathology. Recent research continues to show its advantages over other
imaging modalities because of its cost, portability, dynamic nature, and real-time
guidance of injections and procedures. Orthopaedic residents should become familiar
with musculoskeletal ultrasonography as it becomes increasingly used in
musculoskeletal and sports medicine patients.
